# "The story isn't landing"

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-story-isnt-landing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-07 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: When the story isn't landing, the deck is usually aimed at the wrong audience, built on a category word instead of a buyer, or hiding its evidence too late. Fix those three before touching anything else. The reading conditions make the third fault the most expensive: DocSend's platform data showed average seed-deck viewing time falling below two minutes in 2023, while time on traction slides rose. Three afternoon fixes, done in order, usually change the questions investors ask within two meetings.

## Key points

- "The story isn't landing" is rarely a narrative problem; it is almost always one of three structural faults.
- One deck cannot serve both customers and investors; each reader gets half of what they came for.
- A category word on slide 1 ("a platform for X") stands where a buyer should be; a category sets context but, as April Dunford puts it, does not replace the pitch.
- DocSend's data showed seed decks read for under two minutes on average in 2023, with traction time up 33%, so proof on slide 9 is proof that is not read.
- Do not add market slides, hire a deck designer or cut the valuation to fix a story that isn't landing.

## What it usually means

Founders hear "the story isn't landing" as a narrative problem. It rarely is. It is almost always one of three structural faults.

The first is audience. The deck was written for customers and is being shown to investors, or the reverse. Customers need to know what changes for them on Monday. Investors need to know why this becomes a large business and why you are the team to build it. One deck cannot carry both jobs. When it tries, each reader gets half of what they came for. Investors are explicit about their half. In a survey of almost 900 venture capitalists, Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev found 95% of firms named the team as an important factor and 47% named it the most important; 83% named the business model.

The second is the product truth. Read the one-liner on slide 1. If it says "a platform for X" or "the leading Y for Z", there is a category word where a buyer should be. Categories are for analysts. Investors fund a named buyer with a named problem and a reason to pay now, because that is what lets them judge the business model they say they weigh. April Dunford, whose positioning method is widely used in B2B software, describes a market category as a starting point that sets assumptions about a product. In her words, it "doesn't replace your messaging or your sales pitch." A one-liner that is only a category has not started the pitch.

The third is evidence placement. The best non-founder proof, a paying customer, a renewal, a partner that shipped, sits on slide 9. By then the reader has sat through market size, trend slides and a vision statement. Attention is gone before the proof arrives.

| Fault | Symptom in meetings | Test | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wrong audience | Investors ask about the business; the deck talks about features | Count slides that would matter to a customer but not an investor | A separate investor deck built on one investor belief |
| Category word, no buyer | "Help me understand what this is" | Can a partner repeat the one-liner without notes? | Rewrite as "we help [buyer] do [thing] so that [outcome]" |
| Evidence too late | Questions about traction the deck already answers | Which slide holds the best non-founder proof? | Move it to slide 2 |

## Why the order of slides matters more now

The reader has less time and more choice. DocSend, which tracks how decks are viewed on its sharing platform, reported that average seed-deck viewing time fell below two minutes in 2023 for the first time. Time on traction slides rose 33% at seed and 25% at pre-seed; at seed, "why now" had the third-longest viewing time. These are vendor platform data, not a census of investors, but they describe a reader who skims and stops at the evidence.

The capital is also more concentrated. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, as reported by SiliconANGLE, found that rounds under $100 million drew 12.5% of US venture deal value in the first half of 2026, down from 43.8% in 2024. Fewer dollars are chasing ordinary rounds, so a deck that makes the reader work to find the proof loses to one that does not.

## Where it traces to

This traces to two earlier pieces: [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) and [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/).

[One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) said one product truth, one belief per audience, and a claims register. If the deck does not land, check whether the truth has a buyer in it and whether a belief was ever written for the investor. Most decks skip that step and hope the product sells itself.

[Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) said raise against evidence, not narrative. The evidence log exists so you can lead with the strongest organic proof. If the log is thin, or full of incentivised signals, the deck will feel like narrative no matter how well it is written. That is a different problem, and no rewrite fixes it: the answer is to go and produce better evidence before the next meeting.

> Design makes a clear story cleaner. It cannot find a buyer that is not there.

## The first move this week

Three moves, in order. Each takes an afternoon.

| Move | What changes | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evidence to slide 2 | Best non-founder proof follows the title | Reader believes before they are asked to imagine |
| Rewrite the truth | Remove the category word, insert the buyer and the problem | Investor can repeat it to a partner without notes |
| One investor belief | A single sentence they must accept to invest | Every slide either proves it or gets cut |

Start with the evidence. Pull the log from [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/). Pick the one item a sceptic would find hardest to dismiss. Put it on slide 2, with a number and a date if you have them, and nothing else on the slide.

Then the truth. Write it as "we help [buyer] do [thing] so that [outcome]". Resist the urge to sound bigger. Specific reads as credible. Our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers how to choose the buyer and the alternative behind that sentence.

Then the belief. Write it down, then walk the deck and mark each slide as proof, context or filler. Cut the filler. Move the context behind the proof.

Send the revised deck to the next two meetings only. Compare the questions you get with the questions you were getting before.

## What not to do

Do not add market slides. The investor already knows the market exists or they would not have taken the meeting. If a sizing slide is needed, build it bottom-up from the named buyer, as set out in [What are TAM, SAM and SOM?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-tam-sam-som/), rather than adding another top-down total.

Do not hire a deck designer. Design makes a clear story cleaner. It cannot find a buyer that is not there.

Do not change the valuation. A price cut on a story that is not landing tells the investor you are not sure either. Fix the story, then talk about terms. If meetings are happening but nothing is moving, [The round has stalled](https://lowob.com/research/the-round-has-stalled/) covers the process side.

## How you know it worked

Two signs. First, the questions in meetings shift from "help me understand what this is" to "how do you get more of these customers". Second, at least one investor repeats your truth back to you in their own words, correctly, without looking at the deck.

Illustrative example: moving one slide

Decision
:   Move a named customer's renewal, with its date and contract value band, from slide 9 to slide 2, and cut two market-trend slides.

Reason and owner
:   Meeting notes from five investor calls showed the first ten minutes spent explaining the category, and two investors asking for traction the deck already contained. Owned by the CEO.

What changed
:   In the next two meetings the opening questions were about how the company found that customer and whether the pattern repeated.

Illustrative: a composite of a seed-stage B2B software company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Split the decks.** One deck cannot serve both customers and investors; each reader gets half of what they came for.
- **Put proof on slide 2.** The best non-founder evidence, with a number and a date, before any market slide.
- **Replace the category word with a buyer.** "We help [buyer] do [thing] so that [outcome]" reads as credible.
- **Do not reach for cosmetic fixes.** Market slides, a designer or a lower valuation will not fix a structural fault.

Gateway card

### Before the next investor meeting

- Best non-founder evidence is on slide 2, with a date
- The product truth names a buyer and a problem, with no category word
- One investor belief is written down, and every remaining slide proves it
- Each slide is marked proof, context or filler, and the filler is gone

## Common questions

### Why isn't my pitch deck landing with investors?

Usually one of three structural faults: the deck is written for the wrong audience, the one-liner uses a category word instead of a named buyer and problem, or the best evidence sits too late in the deck.

### Where should traction go in a pitch deck?

On slide 2, right after the title: the one non-founder proof a sceptic would find hardest to dismiss, with a number and a date if you have them, and nothing else on the slide.

### How long do investors spend reading a pitch deck?

Not long. DocSend's platform data showed average seed-deck viewing time fell below two minutes in 2023, with more of that time going to traction slides. Lead with the evidence.

### How do I know my revised pitch is working?

Meeting questions shift from "help me understand what this is" to "how do you get more of these customers", and at least one investor repeats your truth back correctly without looking at the deck.
